quests.word: PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Risk everything on a single plan, with no backup if it fails.
options: GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD
CROSS THAT BRIDGE WHEN WE COME TO IT
PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
quests.explanation: 'Put all your eggs in one basket' means relying entirely on one option, which is risky. "Applying to only one university is putting all your eggs in one basket."
quests.correctAnswer: PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
quests.origin: A literal warning from farming: if you carry every egg in a single basket and drop it, you lose everything at once.

quests.instruction: The intern's writing was messy, but her ideas were brilliant — a real ___.
quests.hint: It describes something or someone with great hidden potential, not yet polished.
options: PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
quests.explanation: 'A diamond in the rough' describes someone or something with real potential that hasn't been developed or refined yet. "He's a diamond in the rough — a little coaching and he'll be a great manager."
quests.origin: Refers to an uncut diamond, which looks ordinary and unremarkable until it's cut and polished to reveal its brilliance.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Approach a problem with unusual, creative ideas instead of conventional ones.
options: GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD
PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
quests.explanation: 'Think outside the box' means to use creative, unconventional thinking. "The old approach wasn't working, so we had to think outside the box."
quests.origin: Popularized in management training in the mid-20th century, often illustrated with puzzles that can only be solved by drawing lines outside a boxed grid of dots.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Act before the right or agreed-upon moment.
quests.explanation: 'Jump the gun' means to start too early, before it's appropriate. "Let's not jump the gun and announce this before it's confirmed."
quests.origin: From track and field, where a sprinter who starts running before the starting gun fires is disqualified for jumping the gun.

quests.instruction: Nobody else wanted to challenge the client's decision, but she ___ and said it wouldn't work.
quests.hint: It means to take a personal risk by saying or doing something others avoid.
options: PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET
GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD
quests.explanation: 'Stick your neck out' means to take a risk, especially by speaking up when others won't. "I'll stick my neck out and say the merger is a mistake."
quests.origin: A literal image from animals extending their necks and becoming exposed and vulnerable, in figurative English use since the early 1900s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Avoid risk by choosing the cautious, low-risk option.
quests.explanation: 'Play it safe' means to avoid taking chances. "Instead of trying something bold, the studio decided to play it safe with a familiar sequel."
quests.origin: A simple, transparent phrase using 'safe' in its ordinary sense — choosing the option least likely to cause harm or loss.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Pursue a mistaken idea or accuse the wrong person.
quests.explanation: 'Bark up the wrong tree' means to have the wrong idea about the cause of something. "If you think I ate your lunch, you're barking up the wrong tree."
quests.origin: From hunting dogs, which sometimes mistakenly barked at the base of a tree the prey had already left, chasing a target that wasn't really there.

quests.word: BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU
quests.instruction: After everything the company did for him, quitting to join their competitor felt like he was ___.
quests.hint: It means to harm or betray someone who has helped or supported you.
options: BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU
quests.explanation: 'Bite the hand that feeds you' means to hurt someone who has been generous or supportive toward you. "Publicly criticizing your biggest client is biting the hand that feeds you."
quests.correctAnswer: BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU
quests.origin: A literal image from animal care: an animal that bites the person feeding it acts against its own interest — used figuratively in English since the 1700s.

quests.word: BURN THE CANDLE AT BOTH ENDS
quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Exhaust yourself by working too much and resting too little.
options: BURN THE CANDLE AT BOTH ENDS
quests.explanation: 'Burn the candle at both ends' means to overwork yourself, often by staying up late and getting up early. "Between two jobs and night classes, she's been burning the candle at both ends."
quests.correctAnswer: BURN THE CANDLE AT BOTH ENDS
quests.origin: A literal image of lighting a candle from both ends at once — it burns out twice as fast, just as a person running on too little rest wears out quickly.

quests.word: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: End up with the worst or most unfair part of a deal or situation.
options: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
BURN THE CANDLE AT BOTH ENDS
BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU
quests.explanation: 'Get the short end of the stick' means to be treated unfairly, usually receiving less than others. "Whoever works the holiday shift always gets the short end of the stick."
quests.correctAnswer: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.origin: Likely from a stick divided unevenly between two people — the one holding the shorter piece clearly got the worse deal.

quests.instruction: After the layoffs were announced, the manager suggested they wait and ___ before making any team changes.
quests.hint: It means to wait until a chaotic or emotional situation calms down before acting.
options: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.explanation: 'Let the dust settle' means to wait for a confusing or upsetting situation to calm down before responding. "We should let the dust settle before deciding who takes over the account."
quests.origin: A literal image of dust kicked up during a disturbance, such as a fall or a fight, which needs time to fall and clear before things become visible again.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately ignore something wrong that you're aware of.
options: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' means to intentionally overlook a problem or wrongdoing. "The landlord turned a blind eye to the noise complaints for months."
quests.origin: Traditionally linked to Admiral Nelson, who supposedly held a telescope to his blind eye during battle so he could claim not to have seen a signal to retreat — a popular but historically disputed story.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Say something that's not quite honest, without a full, direct lie.
options: BURN THE CANDLE AT BOTH ENDS
quests.explanation: 'Bend the truth' means to alter facts slightly, often to make something sound better. "He bent the truth a little on his resume about his job title."
quests.origin: A soft, indirect metaphor treating truth as something that can be twisted rather than broken outright.

quests.instruction: After weeks of denying it, he finally decided to ___ and admit he'd made the mistake.
quests.hint: It means to admit the truth after hiding or denying it.
options: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.explanation: 'Come clean' means to confess something you had been hiding. "She came clean about missing the deadline instead of making excuses."
quests.origin: Uses 'clean' in the moral sense of being free of guilt, a usage traceable to English since the 1800s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Report someone's wrongdoing to authorities or the public.
quests.explanation: 'Blow the whistle' means to expose illegal or unethical activity, often within an organization. "An employee blew the whistle on the company's unsafe practices."
quests.origin: From referees blowing a whistle to stop play immediately after spotting a foul — extended to anyone who stops wrongdoing by exposing it.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Notice the mood of a group of people and adjust your behavior accordingly.
quests.explanation: 'Read the room' means to sense the general mood or attitude of the people around you. "He kept cracking jokes at the funeral — he really can't read the room."
quests.origin: A modern extension of 'reading' as interpreting, applied to a physical space full of people and their collective mood.

quests.instruction: I don't know exactly why, but something about his tone just ___.
quests.hint: It means to irritate or annoy someone, often without a clear or intentional reason.
options: GET THE SHORT END OF THE STICK
quests.explanation: 'Rub someone the wrong way' means to unintentionally annoy or irritate them. "His constant interrupting rubs a lot of people the wrong way."
quests.origin: Likely from stroking an animal's fur against its natural direction, which causes irritation rather than comfort.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Behave extremely carefully to avoid upsetting someone who is sensitive or tense.
quests.explanation: 'Walk on eggshells' means to act very cautiously around someone who might react badly. "Ever since the argument, everyone's been walking on eggshells around him."
quests.origin: A literal image of stepping carefully to avoid cracking fragile eggshells underfoot, applied figuratively to tense social situations.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately ignore or act unfriendly toward someone.
quests.explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' means to intentionally ignore or be distant with them. "Ever since the disagreement, she's been giving him the cold shoulder."
quests.origin: Possibly from an old custom of serving unwelcome guests a cold shoulder of meat instead of a hot meal — a subtle, polite way of signaling they weren't welcome to stay long. The exact history is debated.

quests.instruction: His constant tapping on the desk really started to ___ by the end of the meeting.
quests.hint: It means to irritate someone deeply, often in a persistent, nagging way.
quests.explanation: 'Get under someone's skin' means to irritate or bother them persistently. "His smug attitude really gets under my skin."
quests.origin: A literal image of an itch or irritation lodged beneath the skin's surface, impossible to fully ignore.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Agree completely with someone about something.
quests.explanation: 'See eye to eye' means to be in full agreement. "They don't always see eye to eye on parenting, but they respect each other's views."
quests.origin: A literal image of two people standing at equal height, looking directly at each other — a natural symbol of equal understanding.

quests.word: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Not fully believe something; treat a claim with some healthy doubt.
options: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.explanation: 'Take something with a grain of salt' means to view a claim with skepticism rather than accepting it fully. "He exaggerates a lot, so take his stories with a grain of salt."
quests.correctAnswer: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.origin: Possibly linked to an ancient belief that a small amount of salt could counteract poison, later used figuratively for treating claims with a small dose of doubt. The precise classical link is debated by scholars.

quests.instruction: Even as the negotiation got heated, she calmly ___ and refused to lower the price.
quests.hint: It means to hold firmly to your position despite pressure to change it.
options: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.explanation: 'Stand your ground' means to maintain your position firmly under pressure. "He stood his ground even when the whole room disagreed with him."
quests.origin: A military image of soldiers holding a defensive position rather than retreating, later applied to any firm, unmoving stance.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Betray a colleague or friend by blaming them to protect yourself.
options: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.explanation: 'Throw someone under the bus' means to sacrifice or blame someone else, usually to avoid consequences yourself. "When the project failed, he threw his intern under the bus instead of taking responsibility."
quests.origin: An American phrase that became widespread in the late 20th century; its exact first use is unclear, though the image of leaving someone in the path of danger to save yourself is straightforward.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Do something that goes against the usual or expected way of doing things.
options: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.explanation: 'Go against the grain' means to act in a way that conflicts with normal expectations or one's own nature. "Asking for help goes against the grain for him — he prefers to handle things alone."
quests.origin: From woodworking: cutting 'against the grain' of the wood is rougher and harder than cutting with it, so the phrase came to mean resisting the natural direction of things.

quests.instruction: New recruits are expected to ___ and follow every procedure exactly during training.
quests.hint: It means to comply strictly with rules or expectations.
quests.explanation: 'Toe the line' means to conform strictly to a rule or standard. "Even the senior staff have to toe the line on the new safety policy."
quests.origin: Likely from formations where soldiers or athletes lined up with their toes exactly on a marked line — precise, uniform compliance.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Set a higher standard than before, making things more demanding.
options: TAKE SOMETHING WITH A GRAIN OF SALT
quests.explanation: 'Raise the bar' means to increase the expected standard of quality or performance. "Her presentation really raised the bar for the rest of the team."
quests.origin: From high jump and pole vault, where literally raising the horizontal bar makes the jump more difficult to clear.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Correct a misunderstanding by stating the accurate facts clearly.
quests.explanation: 'Set the record straight' means to clarify facts that have been misreported or misunderstood. "I want to set the record straight — I never said I was quitting."
quests.origin: From official written 'records,' where an inaccurate entry needs correcting, or 'straightening,' to reflect the truth.

quests.instruction: The whole department panicked over the server alert, but it turned out to be ___ — someone just restarted it wrong.
quests.hint: It means something turns out to be a very small or unimportant issue after all.
quests.explanation: 'A storm in a teacup' (also 'a tempest in a teapot') describes a situation that seems dramatic but is actually minor. "The whole office panic turned out to be a storm in a teacup — it was one typo."
quests.origin: A vivid image contrasting a violent storm with the tiny scale of a teacup, in written use since at least the 1800s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: React to something as though it's much more serious or important than it really is.
quests.explanation: 'Blow things out of proportion' means to exaggerate the seriousness of a situation. "It was one late email — let's not blow it out of proportion."
quests.origin: A literal image of inflating something, like a balloon, well beyond its natural size, applied figuratively to exaggerated reactions.
